Pete Hegseth signs memo delivered by drone on Pentagon lawn

The Pentagon, if we let them, will buy a million drones over the next few
years.

You read that right. _One million_.

This spending spree is premised on the Pentagon's frankly dumbass belief that
the next war will look like the one Ukraine is fighting (a trench-warfare
style slog), rather than the kind the U.S. has spent decades and billions
preparing to fight with airpower and long-range precision weapons.

Before I explain why that's (very) wrong, here's how the military came to that
view. As drones shrink in size and AI promises to make them autonomous, the
Pentagon is convinced they won't just shape the future of war but usher in a
completely new way of waging it.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration envisions a Marshall Plan-style program to
pump out millions of American-made drones. As they see it, this will
revitalize the American defense industry and end reliance on foreign
suppliers.

"Do you want to be the victor in the game of drones?" White House
counterterrorism czar Sebastian Gorka said at a Small Business Administration
[event](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TgiE8ByRtzs&list=PLEnS9hOIRR14) last
week, touting the million-drone vision to a bunch of American entrepreneurs.

The future, Gorka explained, "has to be American -- otherwise, we are at the
mercy of others, and we cannot permit that."

Gorka isn't the only administration official hawking drones. In his own
theatrical display, Secretary of whatever he is Pete Hegseth released a video
(see below) last year of himself signing a directive delivered directly to him
by a drone emblazoned with American flags.

" We will deliver tens of thousands of small drones to our force in 2026,"
Hegseth said, adding: "and hundreds of thousands of them by 2027."

He accompanied the stunt with an official memorandum titled "[Unleashing U.S.
Military Drone
Dominance](https://media.defense.gov/2025/Jul/10/2003752117/-1/-1/1/UNLEASHING-U.S.-MILITARY-
DRONE-DOMINANCE.PDF)." While the signed two-page cover memo stuck to broad
rhetoric about cutting red tape and learning lessons from Ukraine, the
Pentagon's accompanying implementation guidance laid out the explicit mandate:
"By the end of 2026, every squad [the lowest echelon of the Army and Marine
Corps] will have low-cost, expendable drones."

Then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll took it even further. He announced that the
Army would buy "at least a million drones within the next two to three years"
-- twenty times the roughly 50,000 it buys annually -- suggesting that it
could buy millions more every year after that.

Then, Hegseth
[unveiled](https://www.army.mil/article/289322/war_department_asks_industry_to_make_more_than_300k_drones_quickly_cheaply)
his $1 billion "Drone Dominance" program: 340,000 small attack drones over two
years, at a price per drone that's supposed to fall from $5,000 to $2,300 at
full production.

By that thinking, the U.S. can buy a million drones even cheaper; hell, buy
enough and the price can be reduced to zero. Before we get to billions (or
trillions, because why not?), it's worth pointing out what a scam this all is.

As long as the Pentagon is throwing around big numbers, let's review: In the
entirety of the Ukraine war, that is, over four-plus years, some 10 million
drones have been used by both sides, which is where the one million (per
year!) is roughly extrapolated. The vast majority of those drones have been
the small "first-person view" (FPV) drones that the Army is referring to.

These are a lot of drones, but this isn't necessarily the future of warfare.
Russia has been resorting to the use of so many drones because it has been
unable to conquer its smaller and weaker neighbor and because it is afraid to
fly its airplanes over Ukraine (or when it does so, it can't coordinate or
carry out a sustained attack). Ukraine, by contrast, has been the model of
self defense. Yet despite the use of these millions of drones, neither side
has been able to shift the stalemate. And the cost in human lives from World
War I-style warfare has been staggering, more than half a million soldiers
killed.

There is no part of this war that we should want to emulate, so the question
has to be asked of the U.S. military: Are they crazy? Do they foresee any kind
of trench warfare with American "squads" shooting a million drones? When their
maximum distance is only three miles? Putting soldiers intentionally in harm's
way just because that's the range of their weapons? Do they forget that the
U.S. has already spent billions upon billions to buy precision artillery and
longer range ground attack missiles specifically so we don't have to put our
soldiers in harm's way? Do they forget that we have airpower, that THAT is the
American way of war? Do we really want to indulge Hegseth and his big-dumb-lug
Army boots on the ground view of the world (or its price tag)?

"The days of $35,000 drones," CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper
[testified](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/policy/defense/4568488/us-
flipped-cost-curve-countering-iranian-drones-cooper/) to the Senate Armed
Services Committee in May, "those days are behind us."

Cooper was talking about the cheap drones U.S. forces faced from the Houthis
in Yemen. The real threat, Cooper said, comes from Iranian drones that are
jet-powered and packed with high-end sensors.

In the current Iran war, Tehran has fired just over 7,000 "one-way attack"
drones at Israel and the Gulf states, and more than 90 percent were
intercepted. Tellingly, when Cooper talked up American drones, he didn't
mention the cheap, short-range quadcopters Hegseth wants a million of. Cooper
singled out LUCAS, which debuted in the Iran war. A long-range knockoff of
Iran's own Shahed-136, the LUCAS gives the military another way to strike
beyond artillery and missiles. At upwards of $35,000 apiece, each one costs
seven to ten times more than Hegseth's "Drone Dominance" models.

In other words, one can buy a flock of cheap small drones -- but what would
they be for, other than to satisfy some obsolete image of warfare of the
future where airpower, space power, and cyber power are absent? Who in their
right mind thinks that? Where is it likely that such a three-mile range
American swarm would even be needed?

Dozens of companies -- small and big alike -- smell Washington's latest
obsession and are only too happy to take our tax dollars to provide the
military with something it wants to buy.

All of this is particularly grotesque amid an affordability crisis, as well as
a war with Iran that in many ways already is the war of the future: a
demonstration that we can hit this target and that one, with little regard for
the fallout or what comes next. That's what you get when the technology is
better than the thinking.

Drone Dominance? How about budget dominance. And some -- literally _any --
_thinking.
